Privacy in RAG Systems
When building a RAG system, privacy is one of the most important considerations. This keeps our data protected and safe from external sources. So let’s dive in.
I’ll explain it with an example. Suppose we’re implementing a RAG application for an educational company, and we’re not using our own pretrained language model (LLM). Instead, we’re using third-party models like OpenAI’s ChatGPT, Google’s Gemini, etc. The issue is that even though they work great, we’re sending our private data to these models, which store our inputs for monitoring abuse or other reasons. Technically, we’re handing over our data to them, and they can use it however they want.
This is a major concern because data from educational companies must be protected. In this scenario, what can we do? As we know, without providing data to the LLM, it won’t give personalized responses and might hallucinate. If we do provide our data, we’re giving away private, sensitive information for free, which they can use to train their models or for other purposes. So what should we do? There are several ways to address this, and I’ll explain three of them here.
1.
Send minimal information
2.
Create a RAG summary index
3.
Keep private data in your backend
Send Minimal Information:
You might be wondering, what does “minimal information” mean? Isn’t sharing any information a concern and considered a data leak? You’re absolutely right, but hear me out. By “minimal information,” I mean providing the context of the query without the actual data. This might sound confusing, but here’s an example.
Suppose we have a user named John Doe, with email john@gmail.com. When passing data to the LLM, we use customer_123 for the name and customer123@gmail.com for the email. This way, we get a response from the LLM without sharing real user data. In short, we’re masking or anonymizing it.
"John Doe" → "CUSTOMER_123"
Create a RAG Summary Index:
This is a pretty simple and straightforward method. Instead of storing full customer details, we store abstracted knowledge or summarized chunks of information. This prevents sensitive data from reaching the LLMs. When we make a request, the LLM only accesses this summarized data, not the actual user information.
Keep Private Data in Your Backend:
This approach is similar to the first method. We don’t share any real data with the LLM—we mask it by sending something like customer_123—and it responds using that. Then, in the backend, we inject (replace) customer_123 with the actual user data from our context. This keeps data from the LLMs while still delivering personalized responses.
User → Backend → Masking → LLM → Response → Backend → Unmask → User
There are many more ways to handle privacy in RAG systems, but these three are the most common and basic ones used in nearly all systems. Implementing these steps in a RAG system introduces another issue: it slightly increases network latency due to the extra steps before returning the response.
In the next article, I’ll cover methods to improve performance and reduce latency in RAG systems. Stay tuned!
